# A common language for statistical models

## The linear model as a sentence

For observation \(i\),

$$
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i,
\qquad \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).
$$

Read this as:

- \(y_i\): the outcome, such as log CFU/mL;
- \(\beta_0\): expected outcome when \(x=0\);
- \(\beta_1\): expected change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in \(x\);
- \(\epsilon_i\): unexplained observation-level deviation;
- \(\sigma\): residual standard deviation.

A t test, ANOVA, and multiple linear regression are variations of this same
framework. The predictor coding and the scientific contrast change; the core
model does not.

## Fixed effects

A **fixed effect** estimates a systematic population-level relationship or
contrast of scientific interest. If temperature is represented by indicators
for 20, 25, and 30 °C, its coefficients compare the expected outcome at those
specific conditions. “Fixed” does not mean the values never change.

## Random effects

For sample \(i\) from tank \(j\),

$$
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + b_{0j} + \epsilon_{ij},
\qquad b_{0j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2).
$$

The tank-specific random intercept \(b_{0j}\) allows each tank to have its own
baseline while estimating how baselines vary across tanks through \(\tau\).
Including tank as a random effect says that:

1. observations from the same tank share a source of variation;
2. the observed tanks are treated as draws from a broader population of tanks;
3. tank-specific deviations are partially pooled toward the overall mean.

It does **not** mean tank is unimportant or chosen randomly in casual language.

Use a random effect because the sampling/design structure requires it—not merely
because a variable has many levels. With very few groups, variance estimates can
be unstable. A fixed blocking effect, generalized estimating equation, or
cluster-robust approach may sometimes better match the estimand.

## Random slopes

If time trends differ by tank:

$$
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t_{ij} + b_{0j} + b_{1j}t_{ij}+\epsilon_{ij}.
$$

Here \(b_{1j}\) lets the time effect vary among tanks. A random-intercept-only
model assumes all tanks have the same slope, which may be biologically
implausible.

## Link functions and generalized models

Outcomes need not be normally distributed. A generalized linear model expresses

$$
g\{E(Y_i)\} = \eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

The link \(g\) connects the expected outcome to the linear predictor:

| Outcome | Common distribution | Link | Coefficient scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuous | Gaussian | identity | mean difference |
| Binary | binomial | logit | log odds |
| Count | Poisson/negative binomial | log | log rate or count ratio |
| Proportion from counts | binomial/beta-binomial | logit | log odds |

Exponentiating a log-link coefficient gives a multiplicative ratio.
Exponentiating a logit coefficient gives an odds ratio.

## Interaction

In \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1T+\beta_2S+\beta_3TS+\epsilon\), \(\beta_3\) asks whether
the sanitizer effect changes with temperature. When an interaction is present,
the “main effect” of sanitizer is conditional on the reference temperature.

## What “significance” tests

Different procedures test coefficients differently:

- Wald test: estimate divided by its estimated standard error;
- likelihood-ratio test: compare nested models by likelihood;
- score test: assess the likelihood slope at the null;
- permutation test: compare a statistic with results under allowed label shuffles;
- bootstrap: approximate sampling uncertainty by resampling;
- Bayesian model: summarize a posterior distribution rather than generating a
  frequentist p-value by default.

These procedures can disagree in small samples or near parameter boundaries.
The chapter for each model explains which procedure is trustworthy and why.
